```plato
    //==
    // # Regularized incomplete gamma functions
    //
    // P(a, x) and Q(a, x) = 1 - P(a, x), following the classic INumerical Recipes
    // `gammp`/`gammq` structure: the power series for the lower function when
    // x < a + 1 (where it converges fastest) and the continued fraction for the
    // upper function when x >= a + 1, each complemented to give the other half.
    // Both evaluations are run to a FIXED depth instead of an epsilon exit —
    // 200 series terms and a 120-level continued fraction — which comfortably
    // exceeds the worst-case term counts INumerical Recipes budgets (ITMAX = 100)
    // for either region. Expected accuracy: ~1e-13 relative for moderate a
    // (a <= ~100); for very large a the split point x = a + 1 costs a few more
    // digits, as in every implementation of this structure.
    //
    // These are the regularized lower/upper incomplete gamma functions cited by
    // the TODO(content) markers on the gamma, chi-squared and Poisson CDFs in
    // `random.library.plato` and `random.library.plato`.
    // https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Incomplete_gamma_function

    // The tail of the lower-gamma power series from term index n onward,
    // where `term` carries the current term value x^n / (a * (a+1) * ... *
    // (a+n)). Seed with n = 0, term = 1/a; the full series then satisfies
    // P(a, x) = exp(a*ln(x) - x - LogGamma(a)) * sum. Converges geometrically
    // once n exceeds x, so 200 terms is far past double-precision saturation
    // for the x < a + 1 region this is used in.
    LowerGammaSeriesSum(a: Number, x: Number, n: Integer, term: Number): Number
        => n >= 200
            ? term
            : term + LowerGammaSeriesSum(a, x, n + 1,
                  term * x / (a + n.ToNumber + 1.0));
```
